title: Conditioning Gaussian Processes on Almost Anything

paper.title: Conditioning Gaussian Processes on Almost Anything
paper.abstract: Abstract Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled probabilistic model over functions, but exact inference is restricted to the linear-Gaussian regime. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, recasting predictive sampling as an ODE with closed-form Gaussian dynamics and a likelihood-dependent guidance term that admits a simple Monte Carlo approximation. In the linear-Gaussian setting, we recover standard GP conditioning exactly; beyond conjugacy, the same machinery handles any conditioning statement admitting point-wise likelihood evaluation — including non-linear physics, and, for the first time, natural language via large language models. Whitening isolates the irreducible non-Gaussian dynamics, minimising Wasserstein-2 transport cost and eliminating numerical stiffness. The result is a general-purpose GP inference scheme requiring no bespoke derivations. Together, these results provide a general mechanism for incorporating the full richness of real-world knowledge as conditioning information, opening a new frontier for the probabilistic modelling of real-world problems.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a fully specified probabilistic model over functions with closed-form conditioning under linear Gaussian observations, offering a rare combination of flexibility and mathematical exactness [ 60 ] . Beyond the linear-Gaussian regime, exact conditioning is lost: non-Gaussian likelihoods and non-linear constraints force reliance on approximate inference schemes such as Laplace approximations [ 47 ] , expectation propagation [ 15 ] , or variational methods [ 23 ] , which are often computationally demanding, sensitive to parametrisation, and difficult to generalise across data modalities. This motivates a framework for conditional GP sampling that treats the problem in full generality, extending beyond conjugacy without bespoke approximations. Our fresh perspective draws on recent advances in diffusion modelling [ 24 , 53 ] and flow-matching [ 33 , 2 , 34 ] , which transport samples from a simple reference distribution (typically Gaussian) through a sequence of intermediate distributions to match a target law [ 28 ] . In diffusion modelling, this transport is described via the reverse-time SDE of a noising process [ 53 ] ; in flow-matching, a learnt velocity field induces an ODE pushing the reference to the target [ 33 ] . In both cases, sampling is realised as an evolution along a path in distribution space. This has led to the realisation that conditioning need not be built into the model from the outset. Rather, sampling dynamics can be modified at test time so that trajectories are biased towards regions satisfying the conditioning statement [ 25 ] , without retraining. Exactness is contingent on three approximations: (i) accuracy of the learned score, (ii) quality of the conditional score along the path, and (iii) discretisation error from the SDE/ODE solver. The main contribution of this work is the realisation that GPs are an exact closed-form instance of diffusion and flow-matching models, see Section 3 . General GP conditioning on arbitrary conditions may then be written as the modification of an underlying analytical transport, and existing conditioning techniques from the diffusion literature can be incorporated see Section 4 . Of the three sources of error mentioned above, the first is eliminated entirely: the GP prior is available in closed form, no score network need be learnt. We prove that the remaining two sources — Monte Carlo guidance estimation and ODE discretisation — are independently controllable, yielding predictive samples at prescribed fidelity with a fixed per-sample cost and without the mixing-time dependencies of MCMC or the parametrisation sensitivities of variational inference. Our contributions offer a new frontier for the GP modelling of practical real-world problems: • GP–diffusion equivalence. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, providing an alternative transport view of GP sampling. • Conditioning on anything. We show that standard linear GP conditioning arises as a special case of test-time guidance, and extend this to arbitrary non-linear, non-Gaussian conditioning via a Monte Carlo approximation requiring only point-wise likelihood evaluations. • Whitening is the optimal parameterisation. We show whitening minimises Wasserstein-2 transport cost, with numerical stability governed by the covariance condition number. • A unified GP sampler. We apply our sampler ( FlowGP ) across applications including constrained regression, physics-informed modelling, Bayesian optimisation, and conditioning GPs on natural language via large language models (see Figure 1 ). • Computational efficiency. FlowGP runtimes range from milliseconds for monotonic bounded regression, to less than 5 seconds for LLM- and physics-constrained generation. In each case, the unconstrained GP produces statistically coherent but semantically uninformed samples, whilst FlowGP produces samples that are also faithful to known physics or semantic content of the text prompt. sections.heading: 2 A primer on Gaussian processes
sections.text: Let f ∈ ℋ f\in\mathcal{H} be a random function in some function space ℋ \mathcal{H} indexed by locations x ∈ 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d \textbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} . The defining property of a GP is that for any finite collection of m m test inputs X ∗ ∈ 𝒳 m \textbf{X}_{*}\in\mathcal{X}^{m} , the random vector 𝒇 0 ∈ ℝ m \bm{f}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} of evaluations of f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) at X ∗ \textbf{X}_{*} follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution 𝒇 0 | X ∗ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( m ∗ , K ∗ ⁣ ∗ ) \bm{f}_{0}\mid\textbf{X}_{*}\sim\mathcal{N}(\textbf{m}_{*},\textbf{K}_{**}) , where m ∗ = μ ⁡ ( X ∗ ) ∈ ℝ m \textbf{m}_{*}=\mu(\textbf{X}_{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and covariance matrix K ∗ ⁣ ∗ := k ⁡ ( X ∗ , X ∗ ) ∈ ℝ m × m \textbf{K}_{**}:=k(\textbf{X}_{*},\textbf{X}_{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} are induced by a mean function μ : 𝒳 → ℝ \mu:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and kernel function k : 𝒳 × 𝒳 → ℝ k:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} . We depart from the conventional notation 𝒇 ∗ \bm{f}_{*} , using 𝒇 0 \bm{f}_{0} to reflect both (i) the standard statistical interpretation of a “true” parameter and (ii) the notation of generative modelling, in which t = 0 t=0 typically marks the data-generating endpoint. One of the most desirable features of GPs is that they remain GPs under Gaussian conditioning with a bounded linear operator [ 40 ] . Let ℒ : ℋ → ℝ n \mathcal{L}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} be a linear operator acting on the sample paths of f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to generate data at locations 𝐗 n ∈ 𝒳 n \mathbf{X}_{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} . Key applications of Gaussian processes conditioned on linear operators in the Gaussian setting include linear inverse problems [ 21 ] ; making inference from derivative observations [ 51 , 41 ] ; data assimilation [ 39 , 10 ] ; and problems involving linear constraints [ 27 ] . Techniques for sampling from GPs . The standard approach is to transform white noise 𝒛 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 m ) \bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{m}) via the mean-scale transformation: 𝒇 0 = 𝐦 ∗ + 𝐊 ∗ ⁣ ∗ 1 / 2 ​ 𝒛 \bm{f}_{0}=\mathbf{m}_{*}+\mathbf{K}^{1/2}_{**}\bm{z} , where 𝐊 ∗ ⁣ ∗ 1 / 2 \mathbf{K}^{1/2}_{**} denotes the matrix square root, raising a substantial 𝒪 ⁡ ( m 3 ) \mathcal{O}(m^{3}) factorisation cost. The SPDE approach [ 59 , 32 ] and its Hilbert space extensions [ 52 ] enable 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ) \mathcal{O}(m) predictive sampling for Markovian kernels via Kalman smoothing; pathwise conditioning [ 62 ] constructs differentiable predictive sample paths as a prior sample plus a deterministic update; sparse approximations [ 43 , 23 , 29 , 61 ] and computation-aware iterative solvers [ 16 , 58 ] further reduce the cost of drawing samples from large-scale GP predictive distributions. These methods and approximations are compatible with FlowGP (Section 4 ) and provide avenues for scalability. Physics-informed Gaussian processes. Kernel-based approaches encoding physics through the covariance structure are restricted to linear PDEs [ 3 , 44 , 8 ] . Modern approximate methods extend to non-linear PDEs — PHYSS [ 20 ] and AUTOIP [ 35 ] via variational inference, and via kernel smoothing [ 11 ] , though the latter yields only point estimates. All of these methods require bespoke derivations tailored to each PDE. Probabilistic ODE solvers [ 50 , 55 ] model solutions as GPs with calibrated discretisation uncertainty and generalise linear PDE solvers [ 40 ] , but extensions to non-linear PDEs remain limited.

sections.heading: 5.2 Solving the resulting ODE
sections.text: In practice FlowGP incurs two sources of error: (i) the guidance approximation, and (ii) ODE solver discretisation. Theorem E.1 shows these decompose cleanly into a guidance error governed by log-likelihood curvature and a discretisation error governed by solver order and step size, which need not compound whenever the likelihood is sufficiently regular. For log-concave likelihoods, including classification, Poisson regression, and convex constraints — guidance error remains bounded or accumulates at most linearly, controllable by increasing S S or reducing step size. Non-log-concave settings, such as mixture models or LLM-based likelihoods, admit only a worst-case exponential bound, though this is likely loose in practice: empirical results in Figure 1 are well-behaved despite this classification. Understanding precisely when this regularisation suffices is an important direction for future work. A full error analysis is given in Appendix E . Non-differentiable likelihoods. A conclusion from Theorem E.1 is that, in order to practically solve FlowGP ’s ODE under genuinely non-differentiable conditions such as binary or equality constraints, we require a smooth surrogate. Therefore, we propose binary conditions (e.g. inequality constraints) are wrapped in a probit likelihood with small bandwidth ν \nu , and equality conditions are replaced by a Gaussian likelihood with small variance σ \sigma , each recovering the original constraint in the limit.

sections.heading: 6 Experimental details
sections.text: We now provide details for four experimental settings, each chosen to demonstrate a key benefit of FlowGP . First, we establish competitiveness with bespoke constrained regression methods (Section 6.1 ). Second, we show that our framework occupies a previously unoccupied position in physics-informed GP modelling, handling non-linear PDEs without bespoke kernels at a fraction of the cost (Section 6.2 ). Finally, we explain how we used FlowGP in tandem with large language models to condition on natural language — a capability beyond the reach of any existing GP method (Section 6.3 ). Appendix I further demonstrates that encoding structural knowledge into the GP predictive distribution via FlowGP improves a down-stream decision-making in Bayesian optimisation. Implementation details. We employ a linear diffusion schedule β ⁡ ( t ) = 10 − 5 + 10 ​ t \beta(t)=10^{-5}+10t and solve the resulting ODE via a simple Euler scheme for 1000 1000 time steps. The SNR-uniform time discretisation of [ 38 ] is used throughout (see Appendix F.2 ); this concentrates steps near t = 0 t=0 where Theorem D.1 identifies stiffness to be maximal, providing a principled justification for this choice in the GP setting. Supported by our ablation in Appendix K , we use only S = 5 S=5 Monte Carlo samples for all guidance approximations. Unless otherwise stated, kernel hyperparameters are estimated by maximising the marginal likelihood on the linear-Gaussian component p ⁡ ( 𝒇 0 ∣ 𝒟 ) p(\bm{f}_{0}\mid\mathcal{D}) before applying our ODE sampler to the full predictive distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒇 0 ∣ 𝒟 , 𝒞 ) p(\bm{f}_{0}\mid\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C}) . Performance is evaluated on held-out test data using root mean squared error (RMSE) and negative log predictive density (NLPD), estimated empirically from 100 samples. Reported timings include both hyperparameter fitting and sampling, averaged over 100 independent runs. All experiments used a Nvidia A4500 GPU workstation except the one-dimensional monotonic experiment which used an Apple M2 Pro processor with 32GB RAM to allow fair comparisons with competitor approaches. Our code will be released soon, with all additional implementation details provided in Appendices G - J .

sections.heading: 6.3 LLM-guided Gaussian processes: conditioning on anything, including text
7 Limitations, future work and broader impact
sections.text: We have established a plug-and-play GP inference scheme supporting arbitrary likelihoods by leveraging an equivalence between Gaussian processes and linear diffusion models, with predictive sampling implemented as a guided ODE. Three key limitations of FlowGP remain. Scalability and discretisation. Cubic scaling in m m makes large-scale problems intractable, and all theoretical results are stated for the finite-dimensional discretisation rather than the function-space limit; a rigorous infinite-dimensional treatment, together with integration with sparse GP approximations and spectral differentiation schemes, remains open. Challenging likelihoods. Theoretical guarantees are strong only for log-concave likelihoods; non-log-concave settings admit only worst-case exponential bounds. Nevertheless, FlowGP performs well empirically across all settings, including those where theory is weakest. We conjecture that Gaussian smoothing induced by the noising process regularises non-log-concave likelihoods in practice. Importance weight collapse remains a plausible concern in high dimensions. Understanding the precise conditions under which these failure modes arise, and developing adaptive remedies is an important direction for future work. Hyperparameter misspecification. Kernel hyperparameters are estimated from p ⁡ ( 𝒇 0 ∣ 𝒟 ) p(\bm{f}_{0}\mid\mathcal{D}) alone, introducing a systematic bias when 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is highly informative. A natural remedy is to optimise hyperparameters jointly over p ⁡ ( 𝒇 0 ∣ 𝒟 , 𝒞 ) p(\bm{f}_{0}\mid\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C}) , perhaps by backpropagating through the ODE solver, though this introduces additional computational cost. Adaptive remedies for prior–constraint incompatibility, such as re-initialising hyperparameters when the guidance term dominates, are also natural extensions. Broader impact . FlowGP is a methodological contribution to probabilistic modelling. By enabling arbitrary domain knowledge — including physical laws, structural constraints, and natural language — to be incorporated into GP posteriors without bespoke derivations, the framework broadens the scope of principled uncertainty quantification in scientific and engineering applications. The main negative risk is that the LLM-guided component inherits biases from the underlying language model, which may propagate into probabilistic predictions in ways that are difficult to audit. Beyond this, we foresee no misuse risks beyond those applicable to GP modelling generally.

sections.heading: Appendix D Numerical Stability
sections.text: We examine two ways to assess the discretisation error from the ODE solver. The first is via stiffness , which provides an notion of maximal instantaneous change in the solution of the linear system. This is an important notion for solvers with fixed discretisation. We will show that this is linked to the condition number of a GP. The next is via transport , which provides a measure of change from the initial to final states. This provides a richer notion of solver error as it characterises the whole path.

Stiffness is a local, trajectory-level property: it reflects sensitivity of the ODE to perturbations. sections.text: When g g is differentiable, ∇ 𝒇 g ​ ( t , 𝒇 ) = ∇ 𝒇 2 ​ log ⁡ p ⁡ ( 𝒞 ∣ 𝒇 , 𝒟 ) , \nabla_{\bm{f}}g(t,\bm{f})=\nabla^{2}_{\bm{f}}\log p(\mathcal{C}\mid\bm{f},\mathcal{D}), so the guidance contribution to η τ \eta_{\tau} is governed by the curvature of the smoothed log-likelihood. By Prékopa–Leindler [ 42 ] , log-concavity of the base likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝒞 ∣ 𝒇 0 ) p(\mathcal{C}\mid\bm{f}_{0}) is preserved by Gaussian smoothing; see also [ 49 ] for a review. Thus log-concave likelihoods give a non-expansive guidance contribution, while uniformly strongly log-concave likelihoods give a contractive contribution on the relevant region of state space. In whitened coordinates, where the Gaussian linear velocity vanishes, this curvature directly controls the sign of the one-sided Lipschitz constant. In non-whitened coordinates, the reversed Gaussian flow also contributes to η τ \eta_{\tau} . Consequently, Gaussian observations and linear inverse problems provide the clearest examples of a strongly contractive guidance contribution. Probit and logistic classification, Poisson regression with canonical log link, and convex-set indicator constraints are log-concave but need not be uniformly strongly log-concave, so they more naturally correspond to borderline or weakly contractive regimes unless additional local curvature is available. Genuinely non-log-concave settings, including mixture observation models, nonlinear forward operators, and the LLM-based conditioning of Section 6.3 , are covered only by the worst-case stability bound. Theorem E.1 therefore gives a unified deterministic perturbation statement, but it should not be read as proving contractivity for every likelihood used in Section 6 .

sections.text: Evaluating sample paths at new test points. FlowGP produces sample paths evaluated on a fixed discretisation grid, whereas the test observations lie at arbitrary locations 𝐱 ∗ \mathbf{x}^{*} . Of course, we can longer guarantee that our condition will hold at 𝐱 n ​ e ​ w \mathbf{x}^{new} , but we can ensure that it is at least consistent with the closed-form GP components. sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: We consider the problem of inferring the angular displacement trajectory θ ⁡ ( t ) \theta(t) of a damped nonlinear pendulum from noisy sparse observations, while simultaneously enforcing that the inferred trajectory satisfies the governing equation of motion. The pendulum dynamics are described by the second-order ODE θ ′′ ​ ( t ) + sin ⁡ ( θ ⁡ ( t ) ) + β ​ θ ′ ​ ( t ) = 0 , {\theta}^{\prime\prime}(t)+\sin\!\bigl(\theta(t)\bigr)+\beta\,{\theta}^{\prime}(t)=0, (69) where β = 0.2 \beta=0.2 is the damping coefficient. The time horizon is t ∈ [ 0 , 30 ] t\in[0,30] s (note that here and below we abuse notation somewhat and let ‘ t t ’ also index our input space).

sections.text: We use a fixed train/test split generated from a numerical solution of Equation 69 . Training observations are noisy evaluations of θ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \theta(\cdot) at irregularly spaced time points. The test set is evaluated on a subsampled grid of held-out time points. sections.text: The ODE constraint ( 69 ) is encoded as a Gaussian likelihood over the pointwise residuals of our target function f 0 ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{0}(\cdot) on our prediction grid t 1 , … , t m t_{1},\dots,t_{m} : r ( t j ) = f 0 ′′ ( t j ) + sin ( f 0 ( t j ) ) + β f 0 ′ ( t j ) , j = 2 , … , m − 1 , r(t_{j})={f_{0}}^{\prime\prime}(t_{j})+\sin(f_{0}(t_{j}))+\beta\,{f_{0}}^{\prime}(t_{j}),\quad j=2,\dots,m-1, (71) with a likelihood standard deviation parameter σ phys = 10 − 10 \sigma_{\text{phys}}=10^{-10} . sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: We consider the problem of inferring the solution field u ⁡ ( x , t ) u(x,t) of the Allen–Cahn equation from noisy, partial observations in an early-time window, while enforcing the PDE and symmetry boundary conditions over the full domain. sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: We consider the problem of inferring the velocity field u ⁡ ( x , t ) u(x,t) of the one-dimensional viscous Burgers’ equation from a small number of observations of the initial condition, while enforcing that the inferred field satisfies the PDE and homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions over the full spatio-temporal domain (as considered in [ 11 ] ). The governing equation is ∂ u ⁡ ( x , t ) ∂ t + u ​ ∂ u ⁡ ( x , t ) ∂ x = ν ​ ∂ 2 u ⁡ ( x , t ) ∂ x 2 , \frac{\partial u(x,t)}{\partial t}+u\frac{\partial u(x,t)}{\partial x}=\nu\frac{\partial^{2}u(x,t)}{\partial x^{2}}, (74) where ν = 0.02 \nu=0.02 is the kinematic viscosity. The spatial domain is x ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] x\in[-1,1] and the time domain is t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] .

sections.heading: Data and experimental variants.
sections.text: We assume we have noisy observations of the initial condition that are generated from the true profile u ⁡ ( x , 0 ) = − sin ⁡ ( π ⁡ ( 2 ​ x − 1 ) ) , u(x,0)=-\sin\!\bigl(\pi(2x-1)\bigr), (75) at uniformly spaced interior points. We consider two experimental settings: • Noisy, scarce data. n = 5 n=5 observations are used, each corrupted by independent Gaussian measurement error with variance σ 2 = ( 0.01 ) 2 \sigma^{2}=(0.01)^{2} . This setting tests the ability to recover the PDE solution from very few, noisy measurements. • Noiseless, dense data. n = 100 n=100 observations are used, with effectively zero measurement error ( σ 2 = 10 − 12 \sigma^{2}=10^{-12} ). This setting tests physics enforcement when the initial condition is almost exactly known on a dense grid. In both cases the observations are 2D input pairs ( x j , 0 ) (x_{j},0) covering only the initial time slice; the model must extrapolate the dynamics forward in time by satisfying the PDE constraint. Ground-truth solutions at three evaluation snapshots t ∈ { 0.2 , 0.5 , 0.8 } t\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8\} are used for quantitative comparison.

sections.text: We place a Gaussian process prior over the 2D field f 0 : [ − 1 , 1 ] × [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ f_{0}:[-1,1]\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} . We use a squared exponential kernel cov ​ ( f 0 ​ ( x , t ) , f 0 ​ ( x ′ , t ′ ) ) = τ 2 ​ exp ⁡ ( − ( x − x ′ ) 2 2 ​ κ x 2 − ( t − t ′ ) 2 2 ​ κ t 2 ) , \text{cov}\!\left(f_{0}(x,t),f_{0}(x^{\prime},t^{\prime})\right)=\tau^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-x^{\prime})^{2}}{2\kappa_{x}^{2}}-\frac{(t-t^{\prime})^{2}}{2\kappa_{t}^{2}}\right), (76) with fixed length-scales κ x = 0.025 \kappa_{x}=0.025 , κ t = 0.3 \kappa_{t}=0.3 , and output scale τ 2 = 1.0 \tau^{2}=1.0 (assumed known, following the benchmark protocol of [ 11 ] ). We construct the GP predictive mean 𝐦 ∗ | 𝒚 \mathbf{m}_{*|\bm{y}} and covariance 𝐊 ∗ ∗ | 𝒚 \mathbf{K}_{**|\bm{y}} on a uniform H × W = 50 × 20 H\times W=50\times 20 grid, giving a base Gaussian predictive distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐦 ∗ | 𝒚 , 𝐊 ∗ ∗ | 𝒚 ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_{*|\bm{y}},\mathbf{K}_{**|\bm{y}}) with m = H ​ W = 1000 m=HW=1000 .

sections.heading: Appendix I Bayesian Optimisation: FlowGP supports well-calibrated decision making
sections.text: GPs are widely used for decision-making under uncertainty, with Bayesian optimisation (BO) being the most prominent example. Certain advanced BO settings benefit from structural constraints: [ 57 ] show that for Bayesian Optimisation with Preference Exploration (BOPE), replacing the standard preference-learning GP (i.e. a probit-likelihood GP that learns via pairwise comparison data using a Laplace approximation) [ 13 ] with a carefully engineered Monotonic Neural Network Ensemble (MoNNE) yields state-of-the-art performance. We consider exactly this setting, but instead of a bespoke architecture, we simply apply FlowGP with monotonicity as a constraint on the standard preference-learning GP. As can be seen in Figure 5 , we found FlowGP (yellow) to significantly improve GP performance (purple) across all six benchmark functions found in [ 57 ] , often matching MoNNE performance (pink). FlowGP thus provides a principled and general way to incorporate structural knowledge into BO, where well-calibrated uncertainty is critical and bespoke architectures are typically required. Lastly, we note that, to the best of our knowledge, there are currently no known ways to encode monotonicity into a preference-learning GP, with FlowGP being the first of its kind. We believe this is a meaningful contribution, since real-world preference functions are often assumed to be monotonic [ 37 ] .

Correspondence to henry.moss@lancaster.ac.uk and l.astfalck@unsw.edu.au Lachlan Astfalck * Thomas Cowperthwaite Colin Doumont Sam Willis Philipp Hennig Christopher Nemeth Andrew Zammit-Mangion Abstract Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled probabilistic model over functions, but exact inference is restricted to the linear-Gaussian regime. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, recasting predictive sampling as an ODE with closed-form Gaussian dynamics and a likelihood-dependent guidance term that admits a simple Monte Carlo approximation. In the linear-Gaussian setting, we recover standard GP conditioning exactly; beyond conjugacy, the same machinery handles any conditioning statement admitting point-wise likelihood evaluation — including non-linear physics, and, for the first time, natural language via large language models. Whitening isolates the irreducible non-Gaussian dynamics, minimising Wasserstein-2 transport cost and eliminating numerical stiffness. The result is a general-purpose GP inference scheme requiring no bespoke derivations. Together, these results provide a general mechanism for incorporating the full richness of real-world knowledge as conditioning information, opening a new frontier for the probabilistic modelling of real-world problems. 1 Introduction Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a fully specified probabilistic model over functions with closed-form conditioning under linear Gaussian observations, offering a rare combination of flexibility and mathematical exactness [ 60 ] . Beyond the linear-Gaussian regime, exact conditioning is lost: non-Gaussian likelihoods and non-linear constraints force reliance on approximate inference schemes such as Laplace approximations [ 47 ] , expectation propagation [ 15 ] , or variational methods [ 23 ] , which are often computationally demanding, sensitive to parametrisation, and difficult to generalise across data modalities. This motivates a framework for conditional GP sampling that treats the problem in full generality, extending beyond conjugacy without bespoke approximations. Our fresh perspective draws on recent advances in diffusion modelling [ 24 , 53 ] and flow-matching [ 33 , 2 , 34 ] , which transport samples from a simple reference distribution (typically Gaussian) through a sequence of intermediate distributions to match a target law [ 28 ] . In diffusion modelling, this transport is described via the reverse-time SDE of a noising process [ 53 ] ; in flow-matching, a learnt velocity field induces an ODE pushing the reference to the target [ 33 ] . In both cases, sampling is realised as an evolution along a path in distribution space. This has led to the realisation that conditioning need not be built into the model from the outset. Rather, sampling dynamics can be modified at test time so that trajectories are biased towards regions satisfying the conditioning statement [ 25 ] , without retraining. Exactness is contingent on three approximations: (i) accuracy of the learned score, (ii) quality of the conditional score along the path, and (iii) discretisation error from the SDE/ODE solver. The main contribution of this work is the realisation that GPs are an exact closed-form instance of diffusion and flow-matching models, see Section 3 . General GP conditioning on arbitrary conditions may then be written as the modification of an underlying analytical transport, and existing conditioning techniques from the diffusion literature can be incorporated see Section 4 . Of the three sources of error mentioned above, the first is eliminated entirely: the GP prior is available in closed form, no score network need be learnt. We prove that the remaining two sources — Monte Carlo guidance estimation and ODE discretisation — are independently controllable, yielding predictive samples at prescribed fidelity with a fixed per-sample cost and without the mixing-time dependencies of MCMC or the parametrisation sensitivities of variational inference. Our contributions offer a new frontier for the GP modelling of practical real-world problems: • GP–diffusion equivalence. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, providing an alternative transport view of GP sampling. • Conditioning on anything. We show that standard linear GP conditioning arises as a special case of test-time guidance, and extend this to arbitrary non-linear, non-Gaussian conditioning via a Monte Carlo approximation requiring only point-wise likelihood evaluations. • Whitening is the optimal parameterisation. We show whitening minimises Wasserstein-2 transport cost, with numerical stability governed by the covariance condition number. • A unified GP sampler. We apply our sampler ( FlowGP ) across applications including constrained regression, physics-informed modelling, Bayesian optimisation, and conditioning GPs on natural language via large language models (see Figure 1 ). • Computational efficiency. FlowGP runtimes range from milliseconds for monotonic bounded regression, to less than 5 seconds for LLM- and physics-constrained generation. Theorem E.1 shows these decompose cleanly into a guidance error governed by log-likelihood curvature and a discretisation error governed by solver order and step size, which need not compound whenever the likelihood is sufficiently regular. For log-concave likelihoods, including classification, Poisson regression, and convex constraints — guidance error remains bounded or accumulates at most linearly, controllable by increasing S S or reducing step size. Non-log-concave settings, such as mixture models or LLM-based likelihoods, admit only a worst-case exponential bound, though this is likely loose in practice: empirical results in Figure 1 are well-behaved despite this classification. Understanding precisely when this regularisation suffices is an important direction for future work. A full error analysis is given in Appendix E . Non-differentiable likelihoods. A conclusion from Theorem E.1 is that, in order to practically solve FlowGP ’s ODE under genuinely non-differentiable conditions such as binary or equality constraints, we require a smooth surrogate. Therefore, we propose binary conditions (e.g. inequality constraints) are wrapped in a probit likelihood with small bandwidth ν \nu , and equality conditions are replaced by a Gaussian likelihood with small variance σ \sigma , each recovering the original constraint in the limit. 6 Experimental details We now provide details for four experimental settings, each chosen to demonstrate a key benefit of FlowGP .
